The reference is a mailbox name and is matched literally: a `%` or `*` written inside it is one of the characters a mailbox name may carry, not a wildcard, so `LIST "100%/" "*"` answers with what sits under `100%/` and not with the siblings a wildcard reading would have reached. The work bound charges each pattern a base cost as well as its length, because matching allocates arrays the size of the name whatever the pattern's length: a pattern of length zero charged nothing while still running a full match per folder, so `LIST "" ("" "" ...)` bought unbounded matching for free. Measured on a thousand empty patterns over a thousand mailboxes: served in full, 487 ms of synchronous work, nothing charged.

items.title: The IMAP mailbox-management verbs, behind an operator-supplied administrator
items.body: `CREATE`, `DELETE`, `RENAME`, `SUBSCRIBE` and `UNSUBSCRIBE` answered `NO ... not configured` whatever the store could do, so a client implementing `DELETE` left an empty folder row behind for every mailbox it deleted. They now work when `create()` is given `mailboxAdmin`, an object whose methods are called as `method(actor, ...mailboxNames)`. They mutate a namespace the client names by string, and on a listener serving several accounts which actor may rename or delete which mailbox is the operator's question, so the listener does not answer it: without `mailboxAdmin` the verbs refuse exactly as before. The listener validates the operands as mailbox names, refuses `DELETE INBOX` per RFC 9051 §6.3.5, and follows the session's selected mailbox across a rename.

items.title: b.mailStore removes, renames and subscribes to folders
items.body: `b.mailStore` could create and list folders and not remove one. `deleteFolder(name)` removes the folder with its messages, flags, search-index and quota rows in one transaction, and refuses INBOX, a folder that is not there, one holding a message under legal hold, and one that is the parent of another. `renameFolder(from, to)` refuses a name already taken, and refuses INBOX, whose RFC 9051 §6.3.6 rename moves the messages and leaves INBOX in place rather than moving the delivery target. `subscribeFolder` / `unsubscribeFolder` record the subscription `LIST (SUBSCRIBED)` reads, and `listFolders` reports it as `subscribed`. An existing store gains the column at `create()`. Every operation that takes a folder NAME resolves INBOX in whatever case the client wrote it, which RFC 9051 §5.1 requires: appending to `inbox` and subscribing to it reach the same mailbox as `INBOX`, and unsubscribing by another spelling removes the subscription rather than reporting success and leaving it. The case is ASCII case, since a folder name is `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+` and a Unicode mapping can only over-match: `ınbox`, whose uppercase is `INBOX`, is a name the store does not hold. A name that is already a row is that row: an earlier version did not refuse `createFolder("inbox")`, so a store may already hold one, and resolving every spelling to INBOX would put its messages out of reach behind a rename and a delete that both refuse INBOX. The reserved name answers only when no row carries the spelling asked for. Resolving the folder and writing its modification sequence read the name the same way, so a mutation under any spelling advances `modseq_max` and no sequence is handed out twice. Every other mailbox is matched by its own case. `renameFolder` keeps the mailbox's `uidvalidity`: RFC 9051 §2.3.1.1 makes that number the one a client checks before reusing anything it has cached, and a rename moves no messages and renumbers nothing, so issuing a fresh one told every client its cache was worthless and discarded the QRESYNC state it would have resumed from. A mailbox created afterwards at the freed name is a different mailbox and gets its own number. A `DELETE` the store refuses because the mailbox holds children is answered `NO [HASCHILDREN]`, the response code RFC 9051 §6.3.5 asks for when a server takes that option, so a client knows to delete the children rather than read the mailbox as undeletable.

items.title: b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey and b.requestHelpers.actorDisplayName
items.body: One derivation of the key that separates one principal from another for a per-actor bucket: an ownership record, a quota, a concurrency slot. It reads `id`, `userId`, `username`, `sub`, `principalId` and `email`, tags each key with the field it came from, scopes it by `tenantId`, and takes an `actorKey` hook for a deployment whose actors carry none of them. It answers `null` for an actor it cannot name, so a caller refuses rather than folding it onto a shared literal, and `ANONYMOUS_ACTOR_KEY` only for the absence of a principal. `actorDisplayName` answers the name to show, reading the same fields in reader order. `ACTOR_IDENTITY_FIELDS` and `ACTOR_DISPLAY_FIELDS` are exported so a consumer can see which fields name a principal.

items.title: b.safeMime.selectBodyParts
items.body: Sorts a parsed tree's leaves into the text a reader displays, the HTML it displays and the files it offers, applying the RFC 2046 §5.1.4 rule that the last alternative is the preferred one. `b.safeMime.extractText`, `b.safeMime.extractAttachments` and `b.mail.server.jmap.emailBodyProperties` all read it, so a stored body, a mailbox listing's attachment facts and what `Email/get` returns describe one representation.

items.title: b.safeBuffer.readQuotedString and b.safeBuffer.previewText
items.body: `readQuotedString(input, at?)` reads one operand of the quoted-string grammar `quoteString` writes, returning `{ value, next }` so a caller walks a line of operands, and refusing an unterminated quote rather than guessing where it ends. `previewText(value, opts?)` renders untrusted input for a refusal message: printable US-ASCII through, every other code point as an escape, capped. The reader lives beside the writer so the two cannot drift apart.

items.title: b.mail.sieve.implementedNames
items.body: Returns the action and test names the interpreter resolves, so `b.safeSieve.parse` refuses an unimplemented name at upload and a consumer needing the same answer reads it here instead of keeping a copy that rots at the next extension.

items.title: b.structuredFields.endsInsideQuotedString
items.body: Reports whether a field value ends with a quoted string still open, counting RFC 9651 §3.3.3 backslash escapes. `splitTopLevel` drops the piece it cannot terminate, so a caller reading that array cannot tell a parameter that is absent from one an unterminated quote swallowed. Ask this before treating a missing piece as unwritten: a grammar whose default for an absent value is weaker than the value being smuggled past has to refuse the field instead.

items.title: A store write is atomic inside a transaction the caller opened
items.body: `b.mailStore`'s multi-statement writes are atomic when the store owns the transaction. Composing them inside a transaction the CALLER opened is a supported shape, and on that path the helper ran the body directly and opened no savepoint: a `deleteFolder` that failed partway left the flag, index, message and quota deletes sitting in the caller's transaction, so a caller batching several mailbox deletions committed a folder that still existed with its messages already gone. The nested path now takes a savepoint and rolls back to it, so the same failure leaves the same state whoever owns the transaction. Whether a transaction is already open cannot be read off the documented contract, which is `prepare(sql)` and `transaction(fn)` and offers no way to ask, so the store asks by opening a savepoint: a backend that accepts one is inside a transaction and joins it, and a backend that refuses one is not, so the store opens its own. The earlier answer read the text of the error a refused `BEGIN` carried, which is a property of one driver rather than of the contract. A backend that answers a second `BEGIN` without raising, as a wrapper that normalizes errors or a pooled handle can, left the store committing the caller's transaction and reporting success, and the caller's own rollback then had nothing to undo. A backend offering only `prepare` reaches the same answer as one offering both. Releasing that savepoint IS the commit when the store opened the transaction, and a commit can fail: SQLite answers `SQLITE_BUSY` while another connection holds a read transaction in rollback-journal mode. The release ran outside the guard that unwinds the body, so a refused commit left the transaction open with its rows pending on the writer connection, the database locked against every other connection, and the next write reporting success inside a transaction nobody would commit. It now runs inside that guard: rolling back to the savepoint undoes everything the store did, and the store returns there, so a refusal inside a transaction the CALLER opened leaves the caller's work and the caller's transaction as they were. The transaction is ended outright only when that rollback itself fails, which is the one state that says the store owns it: only the outermost savepoint's release commits, so a release that fails the way a commit fails was the outermost one. Reading ownership off the handle instead would have left the documented `prepare`-only backend, which reports no state, holding a transaction it could never close: the connection keeps the write lock, every other connection is refused, and the store's later calls open savepoints inside it that commit nothing.

items.title: Vendored bundles refreshed
items.body: `@blamejs/pki` 0.7.45 to 0.8.17 and the public suffix list to its 2026-09-21 revision, both rebundled and re-signed through `scripts/vendor-update.sh` with `lib/vendor/MANIFEST.json` and `NOTICE` updated to match. The framework's runtime dependency set is unchanged: these ship as reviewable source inside the tarball.

items.title: The permissive JMAP profile declares 64 MiB, the largest request it can accept
items.body: `b.guardJmap.PROFILES.permissive.maxSizeRequest` was 100 MiB, and `b.mail.server.jmap` publishes it to clients in the session's `urn:ietf:params:jmap:core` capability as the size a request may reach. No branch honored it: a string body goes through `b.safeJson.parse`, which refuses anything over its own 64 MiB ceiling whatever the caller asks. Measured at the declared limit, a 66 MiB request came back as `notJSON`, "body is not valid JSON", rather than as a size refusal. The profile now declares 64 MiB, which both branches accept, and a test holds every profile's `maxSizeRequest` at or under that ceiling so a later bump cannot publish a number the parser will not honor. The strict (10 MiB) and balanced (50 MiB) profiles are unchanged. A deployment relying on requests between 64 and 100 MiB was already being refused them.

items.title: New options
items.body: `b.mail.server.jmap.create` takes `maxConcurrentUpload`, `maxConcurrentRequests` and `collationAlgorithms`, all published in the session. `b.mailStore.createFolder` takes `owner`, and `b.mailStore.appendMessage` takes `threadScope`. `b.guardJmap.limitsFor(opts)` is new.

items.title: A deployment whose actors carry no id, userId, username, sub, principalId or email
items.body: `b.fileUpload` and `b.mail.server.jmap` refuse such an actor instead of putting it on a shared key with every other one. Pass `actorKey: function (actor) { return …; }` to `b.fileUpload.create` or `b.mail.server.jmap.create` to name the field your tokens carry. Ownership keys are tagged by the field they came from now. An upload staged by a previous version is still reachable by the principal that started it, because a record holding the old untagged value is matched against the old derivation as well, so a resumable upload is not stranded by the upgrade. A record left under the old shared `_anonymous` owner is not handed to an actor that merely cannot be named: those are the uploads the collapse exposed, and they expire on their own TTL.

items.title: A client that matched the old JMAP error strings
items.body: A client matching `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:unknownMethod` and the other method-level URIs should match the bare names instead. A client matching `guard-jmap/bad-json`, `guard-jmap/bad-input` or `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:requestTooLarge` on a refused request should match `notJSON`, `notRequest` and `limit`. A refused request no longer carries `methodResponses` or `sessionState`.

items.title: A misspelled compliance posture now throws at config time
items.body: A guard call naming a compliance regime outside the guard's table throws `<guard>/bad-posture` where it used to run the default profile silently, and the message names the value and the regimes that guard accepts: `hipaa`, `pci-dss`, `gdpr`, `soc2`. A call that names the regime under the option the guard does not read throws `<guard>/bad-opt` and names the option it does read: the command guards take `posture`, the content guards take `compliancePosture`, and each used to ignore the other's spelling silently. Passing no regime is unchanged.

items.title: A mail store that holds more than one account
items.body: Give each folder an `owner` at `createFolder`, or pass `appendOpts.threadScope` on append. Messages written before this carry the scope `""` and keep their existing thread roots; RFC 8621 §3 makes `threadId` immutable, so moving them into per-account scopes means reinserting them with new objectids.

items.title: A caller reading an upload list entry's actorId
items.body: `list()` entries report `ownerKey` rather than `actorId`. The value is the opaque, field-tagged key `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` derives, not the bare id a caller passed in, and the old name said otherwise. Match against it by deriving the key the same way: `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey({ id: "alice" })`.

items.title: A Sieve script that uses fileinto or envelope without require
items.body: Such a script is now refused at parse with `safe-sieve/undeclared-extension` rather than accepted, per RFC 5228 §2.10.5. Add `require ["fileinto"];` or `require ["envelope"];` at the top. A stored script that omits it fails at its next upload or validation rather than at delivery.
